edges.description: Luminal delivery positions motile Aeromonas to interact with the intestinal mucus layer.
Colonization brings bacterial enterotoxins to the mucosal surface, where Act and aerolysin-family toxins can damage host-cell membranes.
Pore-forming Act signaling increases cAMP and COX-2/PGE2-linked eicosanoid production, which favor secretory fluid loss.
Act activates stress MAPK cascades and caspase-dependent apoptosis in macrophages and intestinal epithelial cells.
Secretory signaling increases intestinal fluid and electrolyte movement, producing watery cholera-like diarrhea.
Profuse secretory fluid loss can progress to severe dehydration.
MAPK activation and apoptosis promote inflammatory mucosal damage that can manifest as dysentery-like bloody diarrhea.
Inflammatory mucosal injury contributes to the abdominal pain reported in Aeromonas-associated gastroenteritis.
Proinflammatory cytokine signaling accompanying mucosal injury can drive the fever reported in Aeromonas-associated gastroenteritis.
Mucosal barrier breakdown can permit bacteraemic dissemination from the gut, progressing in a minority of hosts to sepsis.
Species identity and strain virulence modify whether a colonizing Aeromonas behaves as an enteric pathogen rather than an incidental commensal of the intestinal mucosa.
